items.title: Broken Universal Links / App Links Verification
items.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device. Access to the app's assetlinks.json (Android App Links) or apple-app-site-association (iOS Universal Links) file, hosted on the associated domain, and the ability to construct and send a crafted deep link to the test device.
items.whatItIs: The app registers to automatically open specific website links directly (instead of in a browser), but this is only supposed to work once the linked website proves — through a small verification file it hosts — that it actually authorizes this specific app to do so. If that verification is missing or misconfigured, or if the app also accepts the same links through an older, unverified method, any other unrelated app can register for those same links and intercept them instead.
items.rootCause: This link-verification setup depends on a correctly formatted file being hosted at a specific location on the website in question, and any mistake there — a missing file, a wrong ID, wrong file headers — makes the phone quietly fall back to treating it as an ordinary, unverified link that any app claiming to handle it can grab. This can go unnoticed during development because the app might still open correctly on the developer's own test device due to a cached verification result.
items.impact: A malicious app on the same device can register for the same link pattern and catch links meant for the real app. That matters most in security-sensitive flows such as an OAuth redirect or a password-reset link. The attacker's app receives the authorisation code, reset token or other parameters carried in the link before the legitimate app ever sees them.
stepsToIdentify: Fetch the domain's `assetlinks.json` (Android) or `apple-app-site-association` (iOS) file directly and verify it's present, correctly formatted, and lists the correct package name/bundle ID and signing-certificate fingerprint for the legitimate app.

Check whether the app also registers a custom URL scheme (`myapp://`) as a fallback or alternative to the verified App Link/Universal Link, since custom schemes have no equivalent domain-ownership verification and can always be claimed by any other app.

Install a benign test app on the same device that registers an intent-filter/URL-scheme matching the target's link pattern, and send a test deep link to confirm which app's chooser (if any) appears, or whether the test app intercepts it silently.

Review what sensitive data (OAuth codes, reset tokens, session identifiers) is carried as parameters in the app's deep links, since exploitability severity depends heavily on what's actually exposed if interception succeeds.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes installing a test interceptor app on the same device as the target app and sending crafted deep links.
Verify the association-file configuration issue via direct HTTP fetch, or confirm the app falls back to an unverified custom URL scheme.
Install a benign test app registering the same link pattern/custom scheme as the target app.

Send a deep link carrying a representative sensitive parameter (a test OAuth-style authorization code or reset token) and confirm whether the test interceptor app receives it instead of, or in addition to, the legitimate app.
Document the specific association-file misconfiguration (or custom-scheme fallback) and the sensitive parameter type confirmed interceptable.

examplePayloads.label: Fetch and inspect the Android App Links association file
examplePayloads.command: curl -s https://<target-domain>/.well-known/assetlinks.json | jq .

examplePayloads.label: Fetch and inspect the iOS Universal Links association file
examplePayloads.command: curl -s https://<target-domain>/.well-known/apple-app-site-association | jq .

examplePayloads.label: Send a test deep link to the device to observe handling
examplePayloads.command: adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "https://<target-domain>/reset?token=test-token-value"

variants: Association file present and correctly formatted, but referencing an outdated signing-certificate fingerprint after a key rotation, causing verification to silently fail for the current app build.

App Links correctly verified, but the app additionally registers a custom URL scheme handling the identical sensitive-parameter link pattern as an unverified fallback, providing an interception path even when App Links themselves are correctly configured.
mitigation: Host a correctly-formatted `assetlinks.json`/`apple-app-site-association` file with the current package name/bundle ID and signing-certificate fingerprint, and verify its correct retrieval (proper content-type, no redirect) after every signing-key or configuration change.
Avoid registering a custom URL scheme as a fallback for any link carrying sensitive parameters; rely exclusively on verified App Links/Universal Links for those flows.

For OAuth redirect URIs specifically, follow platform-recommended best practice (PKCE, and where available, App-Links-only redirect URI registration) to minimize the impact even if link interception were to occur.
Periodically re-verify App Links/Universal Links configuration as part of routine release checks, since this is a common regression point after signing-key rotation or domain changes.

items.title: Exported Component Exposure (Android)
items.prerequisites: The target application's APK for decompilation. A device or emulator with adb access to send Intents directly to exported components, bypassing the app's own UI entirely.
items.whatItIs: A component of the Android app — a screen, a background service, or a receiver for system messages — is marked as available to other apps on the device without requiring any permission to use it. Any other installed app can therefore trigger that functionality directly. Doing so skips whatever access checks the app's own screens and navigation would normally enforce first.
items.rootCause: Making a component available to other apps is often genuinely necessary — for example, to handle a 'share' action from another app. But that availability was set more broadly than needed, or wasn't paired with a permission requirement limiting which other apps can actually use it. The setting alone doesn't distinguish between 'any app should be able to call this' and 'any app technically can, but really shouldn't.'
items.impact: A malicious app on the same device can call the exported component directly, supplying its own values. That skips whatever access checks and input validation the app's normal screens would have applied first. How bad this gets depends on what the component does. It might only trigger unintended behaviour — or it might be a post-login screen reachable without ever passing the login step, or a data provider exposing files it should not.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and review the AndroidManifest.xml for every declared Activity, Service, BroadcastReceiver, and ContentProvider, noting the `exported` attribute value (explicit or implied by an intent-filter's presence) and any accompanying permission requirement.
For each exported component with no permission restriction (or only a normal-level, not signature-level, permission), assess what functionality it exposes by examining the corresponding code.
Use `adb` to directly invoke each flagged component with crafted Intent extras, bypassing the app's normal UI navigation entirely, and observe the resulting behavior.

Prioritize findings where the exported component reaches security-sensitive functionality (a post-authentication screen, a data-export ContentProvider, a privileged BroadcastReceiver) over one exposing genuinely benign, intentionally-shareable functionality.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes direct Intent-based invocation of the test installation's exported components.
Identify a flagged exported component reaching sensitive functionality.

Construct an Intent (via adb or a benign test app) targeting the component directly, with extras crafted to reach the sensitive functionality without going through the app's normal UI/authentication flow.

Confirm the component processes the crafted Intent and executes the sensitive functionality as proof of concept (e.g. reaching a post-login screen without authenticating, or reading data via an overly permissive ContentProvider).
Document the exact component, its manifest declaration, and the bypass achieved.

examplePayloads.label: Review manifest for exported components and their permissions
examplePayloads.command: apktool d target_app.apk -o decoded && grep -B5 'exported="true"' decoded/AndroidManifest.xml

examplePayloads.label: Directly invoke an exported Activity, bypassing normal app navigation
examplePayloads.command: adb shell am start -n com.target.app/.PostLoginActivity --ez skip_auth true

examplePayloads.label: Query an exported ContentProvider directly
examplePayloads.command: adb shell content query --uri content://com.target.app.provider/users

variants: Exported Activity reachable to bypass an authentication/PIN-lock screen entirely, versus an exported ContentProvider exposing more data/columns than the app's own UI ever displays.

Component correctly requires a permission, but the permission itself is declared at `normal` protection level (grantable to any requesting app automatically) rather than `signature` level (restricted to apps signed by the same key).
mitigation: Set `android:exported="false"` on every component that doesn't have a genuine, specific need to be invokable by other apps.
For components that must be exported, require a `signature`-level custom permission so only apps signed by the same developer key (or an explicitly trusted partner) can invoke them.
Validate and sanitize all Intent extras/data received by an exported component as untrusted input, regardless of the permission model, since permission misconfiguration is itself a common finding.
Audit manifest export declarations as a standing release-gate check, since this is a frequent regression point when new components are added without following the established convention.

links: OWASP MASTG-TEST-0026 (Testing for Sensitive Functionality Exposure Through IPC)

items.title: Hardcoded Secrets in App
items.prerequisites: The target application's APK/IPA. String-extraction and decompilation tools (strings, jadx for Android, class-dump/Hopper for iOS), and, if secrets appear encoded, a scripted approach to test common encodings against extracted candidates.
items.whatItIs: The app itself contains hardcoded secrets — third-party API keys, backend passwords, encryption keys, cloud credentials — built directly into the compiled app or its resource files, instead of being fetched securely at runtime after the app proves who it is to a backend server.
items.rootCause: Developers typed these credentials directly into the app's code or resource files during development, often just to make integrating a third-party service easier — and that practice carried straight through into the version that got published. Since a mobile app is, by nature, distributed to and fully controllable by every single user who downloads it, anything embedded in it becomes effectively public the moment it's published — there's no such thing as a 'private' secret buried inside a public app.
items.impact: An extracted credential gives the attacker whatever that credential unlocks. A third-party API key can be used at the organisation's expense. A backend credential can grant direct access to a database or internal infrastructure. A cloud key can expose far wider cloud resources. Crucially, the same secret is baked into every installed copy of the app, so one extraction affects the whole user base rather than a single device.
stepsToIdentify: Run a string-extraction pass across the full APK/IPA and all bundled resources/assets, filtering for patterns resembling API keys, connection strings, or cloud-provider key formats.

Decompile the application to trace any suspicious string constant back to its usage context, confirming whether it's actually used as a live credential versus an unrelated string that happens to match a pattern.
For candidates that appear encoded rather than plaintext, test straightforward decodings (Base64, hex) before concluding no secret is present.

Where a credential type is identifiable (a third-party API key, a cloud provider key), attempt to validate it against that service's authentication endpoint (only with authorization, and using a read-only/benign check) to confirm it's live rather than a stale/revoked test value.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes extraction and, where applicable, use of any discovered hardcoded credential.
Extract candidate secrets via string extraction and decompilation of the test installation's app package.
For each candidate confirmed to be a genuine, live credential, determine and document the exact scope of access it grants.
Where authorized and safe to do so, perform a minimal, read-only validation of the credential's access scope rather than a destructive or data-exfiltrating action.
Document every discovered secret, its type, its access scope, and whether it appears shared identically across all app installations.

examplePayloads.label: Broad string extraction for credential-shaped patterns from an APK
examplePayloads.command: unzip -o target_app.apk -d extracted && strings -n 12 extracted/classes.dex extracted/res/**/* 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|(?i)(api[_-]?key|secret|token)["'\'':= ]{1,3}[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{16,}'

examplePayloads.label: Decompile to trace a candidate string's usage
examplePayloads.command: jadx -d decompiled_output target_app.apk

examplePayloads.label: Validate a discovered cloud key (read-only check, with authorization)
examplePayloads.command: aws sts get-caller-identity --profile discovered-key-profile

variants: Hardcoded credential shared identically across every installed copy of the app (highest severity) versus a credential that appears unique but is still embedded client-side rather than fetched from an authenticated backend.
Secret embedded in a native library (.so file) requiring native-code reverse engineering rather than being visible via simple string extraction from the managed-code layer.
mitigation: Remove all hardcoded secrets from the app package; supply credentials at runtime via an authenticated backend call rather than embedding them client-side.

Where a client genuinely needs to call a third-party service directly, proxy that call through the organization's own backend, which holds the actual credential, rather than distributing the credential to every client.
Add automated secret-scanning to the mobile CI/CD pipeline to catch hardcoded secrets before they reach a release build.
Rotate any credential confirmed to have been exposed in a shipped app package immediately, since it must be treated as fully public once distributed.

links: OWASP MASTG-TEST-0002 (Testing for Sensitive Data in the App Package)

items.title: Improper Input Validation (Mobile IPC/Files)
items.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device. A means to send crafted input to the app's various input surfaces: Intent extras (Android), file-open/import handlers, and inter-app data-sharing endpoints (a shared ContentProvider, a Share-sheet target).
items.whatItIs: The app accepts input from another app or a shared file, typically through a 'share' or 'open with' action, without properly checking its structure or content. What that costs depends on where the unchecked input ends up. It ranges from a crash, to unauthorised file access, to unexpected behaviour in a completely different part of the app.
items.rootCause: Input checking usually gets built for the app's own normal screens, but not consistently applied to input arriving from other apps or shared files. This reflects an assumption that this kind of input would only ever come from trustworthy, well-behaved sources — not a potentially malicious app or a deliberately crafted file.
items.impact: How bad this gets depends on where the unchecked input ends up. At the lower end it causes crashes, which any other app on the device could trigger. It can also allow reading or writing files outside the intended folder through a crafted import path. Or it can cause logic errors that a malicious app already on the phone can use to steer the target app's behaviour, with no user involvement at all.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate every IPC/file-import input surface: exported components accepting Intent extras, share-sheet targets, and any custom file-format the app opens/imports.

For each surface, craft and send malformed or boundary-testing input (oversized strings, unexpected data types, path-traversal sequences, null bytes) via adb or a benign test app, observing for crashes or unexpected behavior.

Trace how each input flows through the app (does it become a file path, is it parsed by a file-format handler, does it reach a WebView or a database query) to understand what specific vulnerability class a validation gap enables.

Cross-reference findings against more specific, related test cases (the exported-component and WebView findings) since a general input-validation gap is often the root enabler for those more specific issues.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes malformed-input testing against the test installation's IPC/file-import surfaces.
For each surface, systematically supply boundary/malformed values via adb or a benign test app and observe application behavior.
Where a path-traversal-shaped input is accepted via a file-import feature, attempt to read/write a file outside the app's intended working directory as proof of concept.
Where the unvalidated input flows into a WebView or another downstream component, escalate testing toward the specific relevant finding rather than treating this as a standalone terminal finding.
Document each vulnerable input surface, the specific malformed value that triggered unexpected behavior, and the resulting impact observed.

examplePayloads.label: Send a malformed Intent extra to an exported component
examplePayloads.command: adb shell am start -n com.target.app/.FileImportActivity --es file_path "../../../../data/data/com.target.app/databases/app.db"

examplePayloads.label: Test oversized/malformed string input via Intent extras
examplePayloads.command: adb shell am start -n com.target.app/.SomeActivity --es user_input "$(python3 -c 'print("A"*50000)')"

examplePayloads.label: Share a maliciously crafted file to the app's share-sheet handler
examplePayloads.command: adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.SEND -t 'application/pdf' --eu android.intent.extra.STREAM file:///sdcard/malformed_test.pdf -n com.target.app/.ShareHandlerActivity

variants: Path-traversal-specific input-validation gap in a file-import feature, versus a type-confusion gap where a numeric-expecting field accepts non-numeric input used unsafely downstream.
Crash-only denial-of-service impact versus a demonstrated logic-error/bypass achieved through crafted, unvalidated IPC input.
mitigation: Apply strict, allowlist-based input validation (expected type, length, character set, range) at every IPC/file-import input surface, not just the primary UI-driven input path.
Reject invalid input outright with a clear, safe failure rather than attempting to sanitize/normalize it and proceed.
Validate file-import paths against a strict allowlist of expected directories, rejecting any path containing traversal sequences.
Include boundary and malformed-IPC-input test cases in the standard QA/regression suite rather than relying solely on periodic mobile security assessments to surface these gaps.

items.title: Improper Platform Permission Usage
items.prerequisites: The target application's APK/IPA for permission-manifest review. A test device to install the app and observe actual permission usage during normal operation, correlating requested permissions against features genuinely exercised.
items.whatItIs: The app asks for phone permissions — location, contacts, camera, microphone, storage, SMS — that go beyond what its actual features actually need. Maybe a permission is left over from a feature that got removed, was requested speculatively for something that never shipped, or is set to a broader level (like background location) than the feature genuinely requires.
items.rootCause: Permission requests often get copied from a default SDK setup, requested ahead of time for features that were planned but never built, or just never revisited as the app's actual functionality changed over time. Since asking for an extra permission has no immediate visible downside to the developer beyond a slightly longer consent screen for the user, there's little natural pressure to trim the list down to only what's actually used.
items.impact: Extra permissions raise the cost of any future compromise, whether that comes from a separate vulnerability, a malicious update, or a compromised third-party SDK bundled inside the app. Whatever code ends up running inherits every permission the app holds. A data-stealing payload inside an app with background location and contacts access has far more to take than one limited to what the app's real features actually need.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and list every permission declared in the manifest (Android) or Info.plist usage-description entries (iOS).

Map each declared permission against the app's actual, observable features (through normal use and, where necessary, code review of what each permission-gated API is used for) to identify permissions with no corresponding feature.
Pay particular attention to broad or sensitive permissions (background location, SMS read, contacts) and confirm via code review that they're genuinely exercised, not just requested defensively.

Check whether any bundled third-party SDK is the source of an otherwise-unexplained permission request, distinguishing a first-party over-request from a third-party dependency's own broad requirements.
exploitationSteps: This finding is primarily identified through manifest/permission review and code-usage correlation rather than actively exploited by the tester, since "exploitation" here is really a demonstration of the excess-privilege risk rather than a direct technical attack.
Confirm scope authorizes reviewing the test installation's permission declarations and correlating them against actual feature usage.

Where feasible, demonstrate the risk concretely by identifying a separate finding elsewhere in the app (an injection point, an insecure IPC surface) that could be chained with the excessive permission to illustrate realistic amplified impact — e.g. a compromised WebView bridge that could, given the app's granted background-location permission, exfiltrate ongoing location data.
Document each permission found to lack a corresponding, currently-active feature, distinguishing first-party requests from third-party-SDK-driven ones.

Recommend the client adopt a documented permission-justification process for each release, where every requested permission (first-party or SDK-introduced) is explicitly mapped to a shipping feature before the build is published.

examplePayloads.label: List all declared permissions in the manifest
examplePayloads.command: apktool d target_app.apk -o decoded && grep 'uses-permission' decoded/AndroidManifest.xml

examplePayloads.label: Correlate a specific permission against its actual code usage
examplePayloads.command: jadx -d decompiled_output target_app.apk && grep -rn 'ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION\|checkSelfPermission' decompiled_output/ | grep -i location

examplePayloads.label: Check installed app's granted permissions at runtime for comparison
examplePayloads.command: adb shell dumpsys package com.target.app | grep -A20 'requested permissions'

variants: A permission requested for a feature that existed in a prior app version but was subsequently removed, with the permission request left behind.

A permission requested at a broader scope than needed (background location rather than foreground-only, or full contacts read rather than a narrower contact-picker intent that wouldn't require the broad permission at all).
mitigation: Conduct a permission-usage audit as part of every major release, removing any permission no longer backed by an active feature.

Request the narrowest permission scope that satisfies the feature's genuine need (foreground-only location rather than background, a contact-picker intent rather than full contacts-read permission where the use case allows it).
Review bundled third-party SDKs' permission requirements before integration, and prefer SDKs that request the minimal set needed for the specific functionality being used.

Use Android's permission-usage analytics (or an equivalent) in production to confirm permissions granted by users are actually being exercised as expected, flagging unused grants for removal in a future release.

items.title: Improper Validation of Push Notification Payload
items.prerequisites: The target application's push-notification handling code (via decompilation) and, where testing black-box, the ability to send a crafted push notification to a test device — either via an authorized backend test endpoint, or a compromised/spoofed push-sending credential if that's a separate, related finding in scope.
items.whatItIs: The app's push notification handler acts on the content of a notification — like opening a specific screen, or triggering a data update — without properly checking that it actually came from a trustworthy source or matches the format it expects.
items.rootCause: Push notifications are usually treated as automatically trustworthy, since they're normally only sent by the app's own legitimate backend. But if the credential used to send pushes is ever compromised, or if the app doesn't independently double-check the content of what it receives, anyone able to send a push to the app can trigger unintended behavior through it.
items.impact: A spoofed or malicious push message can make the app act with no user involvement beyond receiving the notification. It might open a sensitive screen through an embedded deep link, or trigger a client-side action based on an untrusted field in the payload. In the worst case it reaches a separate parsing flaw in how that payload is handled, turning an unwanted screen change into the start of a more serious chain.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and locate the push-notification receiver code, tracing how it processes the payload's data fields — particularly any that trigger navigation, deep-link execution, or a client-side action.
Check whether the receiver validates the payload's structure/content against an expected schema, or trusts and acts on any field present without validation.
With authorization and access to a test-sending mechanism, send a crafted payload with an unexpected or malformed data field and observe the app's behavior.
Assess whether the push-sending credential/backend configuration has any additional protection (e.g. payload signing) that an app-side validation gap might otherwise be masked by.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes sending crafted push-notification payloads to the test installation via an authorized test-sending mechanism.
Craft a payload with a data field designed to trigger unintended app behavior (an unexpected deep-link target, a malformed action instruction) based on the receiver logic identified during discovery.
Send the crafted payload to the test device and observe whether the app processes it as designed by the attacker.

Where a more serious downstream vulnerability is reachable via the payload (a WebView load, an exported-component-style action), escalate testing toward that specific finding rather than treating this as standalone.
Document the exact receiver logic gap and the resulting unintended behavior achieved.

examplePayloads.label: Locate the push-notification receiver and its payload-handling logic
examplePayloads.command: jadx -d decompiled_output target_app.apk && grep -rn 'onMessageReceived\|FirebaseMessagingService' decompiled_output/

examplePayloads.label: Send a crafted test payload via an authorized test-sending endpoint
examplePayloads.command: curl -X POST https://fcm.googleapis.com/fcm/send -H 'Authorization: key=<test-server-key>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"to":"<test-device-token>","data":{"deep_link":"myapp://admin/reset","action":"navigate"}}'

variants: Payload data triggers unvalidated in-app navigation to a sensitive screen versus triggering a client-side data-mutation action (e.g. silently updating a locally-cached value) based on trusted payload content.
Push-sending credential itself insufficiently protected (a separate, related finding) compounding the impact of an app-side payload-validation gap.
mitigation: Validate the structure and content of every push-notification payload field against an explicit, expected schema before acting on it, treating the payload as untrusted input regardless of its apparent source.
Avoid triggering sensitive navigation or data-mutation actions directly from a push payload without an additional server-side confirmation/re-fetch step.
Protect the push-sending credential/backend configuration with the same rigor as any other production secret, since payload trust ultimately depends on that credential's integrity.
Where the push provider supports payload signing/verification, implement and enforce it on the receiving end rather than trusting transport-level delivery alone.

items.title: Improper Validation of Server Response in Custom Update Check
items.prerequisites: The target application's update-check code (via decompilation). A network intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) capable of modifying the update-check response, and, where certificate pinning is also present, an authorized bypass technique from the related pinning findings to intercept this specific traffic.
items.whatItIs: The app has its own custom system for checking whether an update is available (separate from the app store's built-in one), and it asks a server for the latest version and download link — but doesn't properly verify that response is genuine. It just trusts whatever version number and URL it gets back, with no cryptographic check. That lets an attacker who intercepts or fakes that response redirect the app to install something malicious, or falsely claim there's no update when there actually is a critical one.
items.rootCause: The update-check response is trusted simply because it's assumed to arrive over a secure connection, without any additional signature or authenticity check on top of that. If that connection is ever compromised (especially if certificate pinning is weak or missing, as covered in a related finding), or if the update server itself is compromised, there's nothing else standing in the way of a tampered response being trusted.
items.impact: An attacker who can intercept or fake the update-check response gets two options. They can point users at a malicious update they host themselves. Or they can quietly suppress a genuine security update by always answering that the current version is the latest, leaving users on a vulnerable build indefinitely without ever knowing an update existed.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and locate the custom update-check logic, confirming it exists as a distinct mechanism from relying solely on the official app store.

Trace how the update-check response (version number, download URL) is processed — is any cryptographic signature verified over the response content, or is it trusted based on transport security alone.

With authorization, intercept the update-check response via a proxy (using an authorized certificate-pinning bypass if pinning is present) and modify the version number/download URL, observing whether the app accepts the tampered response.
Test both directions: forcing acceptance of a malicious "update" and forcing suppression of an available update by always returning the current version as latest.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes update-check response interception and modification testing against the test installation.
Intercept the app's update-check request via the proxy and prepare a modified response with an alternate version number and/or download URL.
Replay the modified response to the app and confirm whether it's accepted without any signature/authenticity verification.

Where accepted, demonstrate the resulting impact — either the app proceeding to download from the attacker-specified URL, or the app failing to prompt for an update the tampered response falsely claims is unnecessary.
Document the exact update-check mechanism, the missing authenticity verification, and the demonstrated tampering impact.

examplePayloads.label: Locate the custom update-check network call
examplePayloads.command: jadx -d decompiled_output target_app.apk && grep -rn 'update.*check\|latest.*version' decompiled_output/ -i

examplePayloads.label: Intercept and modify the update-check response
examplePayloads.command: # Burp: intercept the update-check API response, rewrite the version field and download URL, forward the modified response

examplePayloads.label: Confirm the app accepts the tampered response without verification
examplePayloads.command: # observe whether the app proceeds to the attacker-specified download URL or update prompt state

variants: Update-check response tampering used to suppress a legitimate update (a downgrade-attack-adjacent risk) versus tampering used to actively redirect to a malicious download source.
Update-check mechanism present alongside a separate, related finding (insecure in-app update bypassing the official store) which compounds the impact of a successful response-tampering attack.
mitigation: Cryptographically sign the update-check response (version number and download URL together) and verify that signature client-side against a pinned public key embedded in the app, independent of transport-layer security.
Combine response-signature verification with certificate pinning on the update-check channel itself, as defense in depth against both channel-level and application-level tampering.
Prefer relying on the official app store's update mechanism exclusively where feasible, avoiding a custom update-check flow's additional attack surface entirely.

Where a custom update-check is retained for legitimate reasons (e.g. surfacing update availability before the store propagates it), ensure the actual download/install still occurs through the official store rather than a custom, potentially spoofable download path.

items.title: Insecure Biometric Fallback to Weak PIN
items.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device supporting biometric authentication. Ability to disable/fail biometric authentication (or simply decline it) to trigger the fallback flow, and standard PIN-brute-force testing patience (or automation via adb/Frida) if the fallback lacks rate limiting.
items.whatItIs: The app uses fingerprint or face unlock as its main way to protect access, but the backup option — used when biometrics fail or aren't available — is a short PIN (usually just 4 digits) with no limit on how many times someone can guess wrong. That makes the backup path far weaker than the biometric one it's supposed to match in strength.
items.rootCause: A short PIN backup is added for convenience — people expect a quick, simple fallback when biometrics don't work — without giving it the same security treatment as the primary biometric method. Specifically, there's no limit on repeated wrong guesses, which is exactly the protection a short, easy-to-guess PIN absolutely needs to be acceptably secure.
items.impact: Someone with physical access to an idle unlocked device can brute-force a 4-digit PIN in a short, bounded time — at most 10,000 combinations, and usually far fewer given how predictably people choose PINs. Declining the biometric prompt is often enough to fall through to that PIN. With no lockout to slow repeated attempts, they reach whatever the biometric gate was protecting.
stepsToIdentify: Trigger the app's fallback authentication flow (decline or fail biometric authentication) and confirm the fallback mechanism's exact form (PIN length, alphanumeric vs. numeric-only).
Attempt a sequence of incorrect PIN entries and observe whether any rate-limiting, increasing delay, or lockout threshold is enforced after a defined number of failures.

If no lockout is observed within a reasonable number of manual attempts, assess the full keyspace size and calculate the maximum time required for an automated brute-force (via adb input injection or Frida) to guarantee success.
Confirm whether the PIN fallback protects the same sensitive functionality as the biometric primary path, or only a lesser subset, to correctly scope the impact.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes PIN brute-force testing against the test installation's fallback authentication mechanism.
Trigger the fallback PIN prompt.

Using adb input injection (or Frida to directly call the PIN-verification function) automate submission of the full PIN keyspace (or a representative common-PIN dictionary first, for efficiency) without manual re-entry for each attempt.
Confirm whether any lockout engages during the automated attempt sequence, and if not, continue until the correct PIN is found or the full keyspace is exhausted.
Document the exact keyspace size, lockout behavior (or its absence), and the time required to guarantee successful brute-force.

examplePayloads.label: Automate PIN entry attempts via adb input injection
examplePayloads.command: for pin in $(seq -w 0000 9999); do adb shell input text $pin && adb shell input keyevent KEYCODE_ENTER; done

examplePayloads.label: Directly invoke the PIN-verification function via Frida to bypass UI-entry delay
examplePayloads.command: frida -U -n com.target.app -l brute_force_pin_verify.js  # calls the verification method directly with each candidate PIN

examplePayloads.label: Test common/predictable PIN patterns first for efficiency
examplePayloads.command: cat common_4digit_pins.txt  # 1234, 0000, birth-year patterns, etc.

variants: Fallback PIN with no lockout at all versus one with a lockout that's easily reset (e.g. by force-closing and relaunching the app) rather than being persisted server-side or in secure device storage.

Fallback protecting only app-unlock access while a separate, still-biometric-gated action (a payment authorization) remains appropriately protected, narrowing the practical impact of the PIN weakness to app access rather than the most sensitive transactions.
mitigation: Implement progressive lockout (increasing delay after each failed attempt, escalating to a full lockout requiring account-level recovery after a small number of failures) on the PIN fallback, matching the security expectation set by the biometric primary path.
Where feasible, require a longer, alphanumeric passcode rather than a 4-digit numeric PIN for the fallback, increasing the keyspace substantially.

Persist the failed-attempt counter in secure, tamper-resistant storage (not easily resettable by force-closing the app or clearing app data without additional friction) so lockout state survives simple bypass attempts.
Ensure the fallback path protects exactly the same scope of sensitive functionality as the biometric primary path, so a successful fallback compromise doesn't grant disproportionately broad access.

links: CWE-307 (Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts)

items.title: Insecure Handling of App Widget Data Exposure (Android)
items.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device, configured with a home-screen widget if the app provides one. Standard device inspection (viewing the lock screen with the widget present, or, for a rooted device, inspecting the widget's rendering/data source directly).
items.whatItIs: A home-screen widget shows sensitive information directly — account balances, recent messages, personal details — including in situations where that widget is visible on the lock screen before the phone is even unlocked, exposing that data to anyone who can just glance at the screen.
items.rootCause: Widgets exist to show useful info at a glance without opening the full app, and the convenience of doing that was prioritized without considering that widgets can be visible on the lock screen — a place where the same information would normally require unlocking the phone and opening the app to see.
items.impact: Anyone near the device can read the information straight from the lock screen. That includes a bystander, someone who found or stole the phone, or a person glancing over in a public place. No authentication is required at any point, which defeats the app's own login controls entirely for whatever the widget chooses to display.
stepsToIdentify: Install the app's widget on the test device's home screen and populate it with representative sensitive data through normal app use.

Lock the device and observe whether the widget remains visible (and displaying the sensitive data) on the lock screen, versus being hidden or showing only a generic placeholder until the device is unlocked.
Where the widget does hide content pre-unlock, verify this behavior is consistent across all data fields the widget can display, not just the most obviously sensitive one.

Check the widget's configuration options (if any) for a user-controllable setting to hide sensitive content on the lock screen, and assess whether it defaults to the more private or more exposed state.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes lock-screen widget inspection on the test installation.
Configure the widget with representative sensitive test data.
Lock the device and observe/document exactly what sensitive data remains visible on the widget without unlocking.
Where a privacy-mode setting exists, test both its enabled and disabled states to characterize the full range of exposure.
Document the specific data fields exposed pre-unlock and any available (or absent) user-facing mitigation setting.

examplePayloads.label: Populate the widget with test data and lock the device to observe lock-screen visibility
examplePayloads.command: # add the app's widget to the home screen, populate representative sensitive test data, then lock the device and photograph/inspect the lock-screen widget state

examplePayloads.label: Inspect widget provider content for sensitive data exposure
examplePayloads.command: adb shell dumpsys appwidget | grep -A5 '<target-package>'

variants: Widget exposing sensitive data on the lock screen by default with an opt-in privacy setting the user must discover and enable, versus offering no privacy setting at all.
Widget correctly hiding primary account data but still leaking secondary sensitive metadata (a notification count implying account activity, for example) even in its privacy-conscious state.
mitigation: Default the widget to a privacy-conscious state on the lock screen, showing only generic/non-sensitive placeholder content until the device is unlocked, with an explicit opt-in required to show more.
Where the platform distinguishes lock-screen visibility from home-screen (unlocked) visibility, use that distinction to show full detail only in the unlocked context.
Avoid exposing any data via the widget that the app itself would otherwise require authentication to view within its own UI.
Periodically review widget content for new fields added in later releases, ensuring the same privacy-conscious defaults are maintained as functionality evolves.

links: OWASP MASTG-TEST-0029 (Testing for Sensitive Data Disclosure Through the User Interface)

items.title: Insecure In-App Update Mechanism Bypassing Official Store
items.prerequisites: The target application's update mechanism (if it implements a custom, non-store-based update flow). A network intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) to intercept and modify the update-package download, and a benign proof-of-concept APK/IPA to substitute in place of the legitimate update.
items.whatItIs: The app has its own system for downloading and installing updates outside of the official app store — common for internal/enterprise apps — and that custom update system doesn't properly check that the downloaded file is genuine and untampered (a real signature check against the vendor's known key) before installing it. On Android, this sometimes means requesting permission to install packages directly and installing them with no signature check at all.
items.rootCause: Skipping the official app store's update system also means giving up the free, built-in signature verification the store normally provides. If the custom update system doesn't rebuild an equivalent check on its own, the downloaded update is trusted just because it came from the expected web address over a (hopefully) secure connection — a much weaker guarantee than a real cryptographic signature check.
items.impact: An attacker who can intercept the update download, or who has compromised the distribution server, can deliver any app package they choose. The user is prompted to install it and has every reason to believe it is a genuine update, since it arrives through the vendor's own update process. The result is full device compromise, with whatever permissions the substituted app requests.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the app implements a custom, non-store update mechanism (rather than deferring entirely to the platform's official app-store update flow).

Decompile the app to trace the update-download and installation code path, checking whether any cryptographic signature verification occurs against the downloaded package before the install prompt is triggered.

With authorization, intercept the update-download traffic via a proxy and substitute a different, clearly-labeled benign test package, observing whether the app proceeds to prompt for its installation.

Check whether the app checks the downloaded package's certificate/signature against a pinned, expected value (not just checking that a signature exists at all, which any self-signed package would trivially satisfy).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes update-package interception and substitution testing against the test installation.
Trigger the app's update-check/download flow.
Intercept the download via the proxy and substitute a benign, clearly-labeled proof-of-concept package in place of the legitimate update.
Observe whether the app proceeds to the installation prompt for the substituted package without any signature-mismatch warning.
Document the exact verification gap (no check, or a check that doesn't validate against the vendor's actual expected signing key) and the resulting installation-prompt behavior.

examplePayloads.label: Intercept the update-package download and substitute a benign test package
examplePayloads.command: # Burp: intercept the update-download response, replace the response body with a benign, clearly-labeled proof-of-concept APK

examplePayloads.label: Check for REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES usage and any signature-verification call around it
examplePayloads.command: jadx -d decompiled_output target_app.apk && grep -rn 'REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES\|PackageManager.getPackageArchiveInfo' decompiled_output/

variants: No signature verification at all versus a verification step that only confirms *a* valid signature exists (satisfied trivially by any self-signed package) rather than matching against the vendor's specific, pinned signing certificate.
Update mechanism used for enterprise/internal distribution outside any app store, where the organization's own security posture (rather than a third party's) is entirely responsible for this control.
mitigation: Verify the downloaded update package's signature against the vendor's specific, pinned signing certificate before prompting installation, rejecting any package that doesn't match exactly.
Serve the update-download channel over TLS with certificate pinning, in addition to package-signature verification, as defense in depth.

Prefer distributing and updating through the official app store wherever policy allows, since this provides package-signature verification as a built-in, already-hardened platform feature rather than requiring a custom re-implementation.

For enterprise/MDM-distributed apps where a custom update channel is unavoidable, leverage the MDM platform's own package-integrity verification features rather than building a bespoke, potentially weaker mechanism.

reference.standard: A08:2021 - Software and Data Integrity Failures

items.title: Insecure Inter-App Data Sharing
items.prerequisites: The target application and a second, benign test app installed on the same test device, both authored/controlled by the tester if inter-app data sharing needs to be simulated. Standard IPC-inspection tooling (adb, Frida) to observe shared data.
items.whatItIs: The app shares data with other apps on the phone — through a shared storage mechanism, a shared file, or a broadcast message — in a way that exposes more data, or exposes it to more apps, than the specific feature it's meant for actually requires.
items.rootCause: This kind of sharing is usually built to support one specific, legitimate need — like sharing a document with another app, or syncing with a companion app from the same company. But the sharing mechanism ends up configured more broadly than that one use case needs, often because narrowing it down (to just that one verified companion app, for example) takes more deliberate setup than a general-purpose, open sharing method.
items.impact: Any app on the device can reach the shared data, not only the companion app the feature was built for. The exposed data often includes more fields than the feature's visible purpose would suggest. What was meant as a narrow integration with one trusted partner becomes an open channel to whatever the user happens to have installed, including something malicious.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the app's inter-app data-sharing mechanisms (an exported ContentProvider, files placed in a shared location, custom broadcast intents carrying data) via manifest and code review.
For each mechanism, determine what data fields are actually included versus what the feature's user-facing purpose requires.

Check whether access is restricted to a specific, expected companion app (via a signature-level permission or an explicit package-name check) or is open to any app that knows the sharing mechanism's interface.
From a separate, benign test app with no special permissions, attempt to access the shared data to confirm real-world cross-app accessibility.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cross-app data-access testing between the test installation and a separate, benign test app on the same device.
From the benign test app, attempt to access the identified sharing mechanism (query the ContentProvider, read the shared file, listen for the broadcast).
Confirm what data is retrievable and whether it exceeds what the sharing feature's advertised purpose requires.
Document the exact sharing mechanism, its actual access scope, and the specific excess data fields exposed.

Recommend restricting the sharing mechanism to signature-level permission (same developer/organization signing key) or explicit package-name allowlisting, rather than leaving it open to any installed app.

examplePayloads.label: Query a shared ContentProvider from a separate test app/adb
examplePayloads.command: adb shell content query --uri content://com.target.app.shareprovider/data

examplePayloads.label: Check a shared file's location and permissions
examplePayloads.command: adb shell ls -la /storage/emulated/0/Android/data/com.target.app/shared/

examplePayloads.label: Listen for a custom inter-app broadcast carrying shared data
examplePayloads.command: adb shell am broadcast -a com.target.app.DATA_SYNC  # trigger, then inspect a registered test-app receiver's logged extras

variants: Sharing mechanism correctly restricted to a specific companion app via signature-level permission, but the companion app itself then re-exposes the same data more broadly through its own, separately-reviewed component.
Shared file placed in a location with overly broad file-system permissions rather than the sharing mechanism's access-control logic itself being at fault.
mitigation: Restrict inter-app data-sharing mechanisms to the specific, intended companion app using a signature-level permission or an explicit, verified package-name/signature check, rather than a broadly-accessible mechanism.
Share only the minimal data fields the specific integration use case requires, rather than the complete underlying data record.

Where the sharing mechanism is a ContentProvider, apply the same least-privilege data-scoping (specific columns/rows) that a well-designed API would apply, rather than exposing broad, unfiltered query access.

Periodically review inter-app sharing mechanisms for scope creep, since new data fields are sometimes added to an existing shared record without re-evaluating whether they belong in the shared scope at all.

links: CWE-926 (Improper Export of Android Application Components)

items.title: Insecure Keychain/Keystore Usage
items.prerequisites: The target application installed on a rooted/jailbroken test device with Frida available. A decompiler to locate Keychain/Keystore API usage and its configured access-control attributes.
items.whatItIs: The app stores something sensitive (a login token, an encryption key) in the phone's secure credential storage — but sets it up too loosely, like not requiring the phone to actually be unlocked to retrieve it, or not requiring a fingerprint/passcode check when accessing it. So even though the secure storage system is being used, its actual protection is much weaker than it could be.
items.rootCause: Just using the phone's secure storage system is often treated as good enough by itself, without the extra step of configuring exactly how protected each stored item should be. The default settings for these systems often don't require an unlock or biometric check unless the developer specifically asks for that — so simply calling the secure-storage function without extra configuration gives a much weaker guarantee than the phone is actually capable of providing.
items.impact: Depending on the exact gap, an attacker with a rooted or jailbroken device, or one who pulls a backup or device image, may retrieve the stored secret without unlocking the phone or passing biometrics at all. That leaves the practical protection close to what ordinary storage would have given. The app nominally follows the 'use the secure store' best practice, but the setting that makes it meaningful is missing.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and locate every Keychain (iOS) or Android Keystore item-generation/storage call, reviewing the specific accessibility/access-control attributes configured for each.

For iOS, check whether the Keychain item's accessibility constant is a restrictive one (`kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly` or stricter, ideally paired with a biometric access-control flag) versus a looser default.

For Android, check whether the Keystore key was generated with `setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)` and an appropriate validity duration, or whether it's usable without any authentication check at retrieval time.

With authorization on a rooted/jailbroken device, attempt to retrieve the stored item directly (via Frida hooking the retrieval call, or direct Keychain/Keystore inspection tooling) without providing device unlock/biometric confirmation, to confirm the gap is practically exploitable and not just a theoretical configuration concern.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes Keychain/Keystore item extraction testing on a rooted/jailbroken test device.
Identify the specific stored item and its configured access-control attributes via decompilation.
Attempt retrieval of the stored item using Frida or direct secure-storage inspection tooling, without providing device unlock/biometric confirmation.
Confirm whether retrieval succeeds despite the absence of the expected authentication step.
Document the exact item, its configured (insufficient) access-control attribute, and the successful bypass achieved.

examplePayloads.label: Search decompiled code for Keychain/Keystore item generation and its access-control configuration
examplePayloads.command: jadx -d decompiled_output target_app.apk && grep -rn 'setUserAuthenticationRequired\|KeyGenParameterSpec' decompiled_output/

examplePayloads.label: Attempt direct retrieval of a stored Keychain item on a jailbroken device
examplePayloads.command: # via a jailbreak-device Keychain-dumping tool (e.g. keychain-dumper) to list items and their accessibility attributes

examplePayloads.label: Hook the app's own retrieval call via Frida to confirm no authentication prompt is enforced
examplePayloads.command: frida -U -n com.target.app -l hook_keystore_retrieval.js

variants: iOS Keychain item stored with an overly permissive accessibility constant (retrievable even when the device is locked) versus an Android Keystore key missing the user-authentication-required flag entirely.
Access-control attribute correctly configured for one sensitive item but inconsistently applied to another, equally sensitive item stored via the same API elsewhere in the app.
mitigation: Configure every Keychain item with the most restrictive accessibility constant appropriate to its use (`kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly` at minimum, combined with a biometric access-control flag for the most sensitive items).
Generate every Android Keystore key intended to protect sensitive data with `setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)` and an appropriately short authentication-validity duration.
Audit all secure-storage API usage for consistent application of these access-control attributes across every sensitive item the app stores, not just the most obviously critical one.

Periodically re-test secure-storage configuration on a rooted/jailbroken device as part of routine mobile security assessments, since this class of gap is easy to introduce when a new sensitive field is added without following the established, more restrictive convention.

items.title: Insecure URL Scheme / Deep Link Handling
items.prerequisites: The target application's manifest/Info.plist for custom URL-scheme registration review. A means to send a crafted URL to the test device (adb, or a link within a test web page/another app) targeting the registered scheme.
items.whatItIs: The app registers its own custom link format, such as 'myapp://', to handle certain actions. The code processing an incoming link does not properly check where that link came from before acting on it. It will accept sensitive actions — logging in, changing a setting — purely because a link said so, with no confirmation the link came from a trusted source rather than any random app or webpage.
items.rootCause: Custom link formats like this have no built-in way to prove which website or app is actually allowed to send them — unlike the newer, verified link system covered in a related finding. Any app on the phone, or any webpage in any browser, can build and trigger one of these links with whatever parameters it wants. If the app's handler trusts those parameters to perform something sensitive without double-checking where they came from, that link format becomes an open door anyone can knock on.
items.impact: Any malicious app, or any web page the victim visits, can trigger the sensitive action the custom link exposes. If that link is used as an OAuth-style callback without proper origin checks, it can silently sign the user into an account the attacker controls. It may also fire an unwanted in-app action, or change state outright — altering a setting or starting a transaction — purely because the victim clicked a link, with no informed consent to that specific action.
stepsToIdentify: Review the app's manifest/Info.plist for every registered custom URL scheme and decompile the corresponding handler code to understand what actions each URL path/parameter combination triggers.

Identify any handler that performs a sensitive, state-changing action (not just navigation to a screen) directly from URL parameters without an additional confirmation step or origin/source validation.

Craft a test URL replicating the sensitive action's parameter structure and trigger it via adb, a test web page, or a benign test app, observing whether the action executes without any additional user confirmation or source check.
Where the scheme is used for an OAuth-style redirect/callback, check specifically for state-parameter validation to rule out authorization-code interception/injection via this channel.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes sending crafted custom-URL-scheme links to the test installation.
Identify a sensitive action reachable via the custom scheme's handler, based on the decompiled logic.
Construct a test URL replicating that action's expected parameters.
Trigger the URL via adb or a benign test web page/app and confirm the sensitive action executes without additional user confirmation or origin validation.
Document the exact URL scheme, path/parameters, and the sensitive action achieved without proper authorization.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate registered custom URL schemes
examplePayloads.command: apktool d target_app.apk -o decoded && grep -B5 -A5 'scheme=' decoded/AndroidManifest.xml

examplePayloads.label: Trigger a crafted deep link via adb
examplePayloads.command: adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "myapp://action/transfer?amount=100&to=attacker_account"

examplePayloads.label: Trigger the same link from a test web page to demonstrate a fully remote trigger
examplePayloads.command: echo 'Click' > poc.html

variants: Custom scheme used as an OAuth redirect URI without state-parameter validation, enabling authorization-code interception/injection distinct from a direct sensitive-action trigger.

Sensitive action reachable via the custom scheme but requiring the app to already be in a specific, pre-authenticated session state, narrowing (but not eliminating) the practical attack window compared to a fully unauthenticated trigger.
mitigation: Require an additional, explicit user confirmation step within the app before executing any sensitive, state-changing action triggered via a custom URL scheme, regardless of the parameters supplied.
Prefer Android App Links/iOS Universal Links (which verify domain ownership) over custom URL schemes for any deep link that triggers sensitive functionality.
For OAuth-style flows, always validate the `state` parameter and use PKCE to prevent authorization-code interception/injection via the custom scheme.
Treat all custom-URL-scheme parameters as untrusted, externally-controllable input requiring the same validation rigor as any other unauthenticated input source.

items.title: Insufficient Anti-Tampering Against Repackaging (Android APK Resigning)
items.prerequisites: The target application's APK. Standard Android tooling to decompile, modify, and re-sign an APK (apktool, apksigner or jarsigner with a self-generated test key) and a test device/emulator with developer options enabled to sideload the modified package.
items.whatItIs: The Android app can be taken apart, modified — say, to remove a security check or license verification — and re-signed with a completely different key, then reinstalled and run, all without the app or its backend ever noticing it's no longer the real, original app. That's because the app never checks its own signature against what it should actually be.
items.rootCause: Android allows any app package to be re-signed with any key and installed, as long as the user allows installs from outside the store. Unless the app specifically checks its own signature at runtime against a known-good value, there's nothing stopping a modified, re-signed copy of it from running — and the backend it talks to has no way to tell the difference either.
items.impact: An attacker can repackage the app with security checks stripped out, malicious code added, or licence and purchase validation removed, then distribute it through a third-party store or direct download. Users installing it have no way to tell it is not the official build. Any resulting credential theft, malware or fraud happens under the cover of the real app's name and branding.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and search for any runtime self-verification of its own signing certificate (comparing `PackageManager` signature info against an expected, hardcoded value).

If no such check is found, attempt to fully repackage the app: decompile with apktool, make a benign, easily-identifiable modification (e.g. a UI text change), and re-sign the resulting APK with a self-generated test key.
Install the repackaged, differently-signed APK on a test device and confirm whether it runs normally (or with the injected modification active) without any detection or refusal to run.

Where a signature-verification check does exist, assess its robustness — is it a simple, unobfuscated comparison that's itself trivially patchable out via the same repackaging process, or does it employ additional anti-tampering protection.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes decompiling, modifying, re-signing, and running a repackaged version of the test installation.
Decompile the app, make a benign, clearly-identifiable modification (for demonstration purposes, not a genuinely malicious payload), and re-sign the resulting package with a test key.
Install the repackaged APK on a test device and confirm it launches and operates normally, with the injected modification active, despite the certificate mismatch from the original.

Where the app communicates with a backend, confirm the backend also has no server-side signature/attestation check (such as Play Integrity API) that would otherwise detect and reject the repackaged client.
Document the exact absence (or bypassability) of self-verification, and the resulting successful execution of the repackaged app.

examplePayloads.label: Decompile, modify, and repackage the APK
examplePayloads.command:
apktool d target_app.apk -o modified_app
# make a benign modification to modified_app/smali or resources
apktool b modified_app -o repackaged.apk

examplePayloads.label: Re-sign the repackaged APK with a test key
examplePayloads.command:
keytool -genkey -v -keystore test.keystore -alias testkey -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000
apksigner sign --ks test.keystore --out repackaged_signed.apk repackaged.apk

examplePayloads.label: Install and run the repackaged, differently-signed APK
examplePayloads.command: adb install repackaged_signed.apk

variants: Repackaging used to remove a license/anti-piracy check versus repackaging used to inject genuinely malicious code (a credential-harvesting overlay) while preserving the app's original, legitimate-looking functionality and branding.
App-side signature check present but only enforced at one entry point, bypassable by patching out that specific check without needing to defeat any broader anti-tampering scheme.
mitigation: Implement runtime self-verification of the app's own signing certificate against an expected, embedded value, refusing to run (or degrading functionality) if a mismatch is detected.

Use the platform's official integrity-attestation service (Google Play Integrity API, Apple's App Attest) to have the backend independently verify the client's authenticity server-side, rather than relying solely on client-side self-checks that can themselves be patched out.

Apply code obfuscation and anti-tampering protection specifically hardening the signature-verification logic itself, so it can't simply be patched out via the same repackaging process used to defeat other checks.
Monitor third-party app stores and known piracy/repackaging distribution channels for unauthorized, modified versions of the app circulating in the wild.

items.title: Insufficient Binary Protection (No Obfuscation/RASP)
items.prerequisites: The target application's APK/IPA. A decompiler (jadx, Ghidra, class-dump/Hopper) and a debugger/instrumentation framework (Frida, x64dbg-equivalent for mobile via jdb, or an iOS jailbreak debugger) to assess how readily the app yields to standard static and dynamic analysis.
items.whatItIs: The app ships with absolutely no protection against being analyzed or tampered with — no code obfuscation, no anti-debugging, no detection of rooted/jailbroken phones. Taking it apart reveals fully readable, near-original logic, and a debugger or tampering tool can attach to the running app with zero resistance.
items.rootCause: This kind of protection just wasn't prioritized during development — either the team didn't think reverse-engineering resistance mattered for this particular app, or building it in (through a commercial tool, or custom anti-debugging code) got pushed aside in favor of shipping features faster. The result is an app that's just as easy to analyze and modify as an unfinished development build.
items.impact: The absence of binary protection lowers the effort for nearly every other client-side attack on this list — tampering with business logic, extracting hardcoded secrets, bypassing pinning, defeating the biometric gate, repackaging the app. None of them need to defeat an anti-tampering layer first, because there isn't one. This finding is best understood as a multiplier on the app's other findings rather than something exploitable on its own.
stepsToIdentify: Attempt straightforward decompilation of the app and assess how close the output is to readable, near-original source code.
Attempt to attach a debugger/instrumentation framework (Frida) to a running instance and confirm no anti-debugging countermeasure triggers.

Check for any root/jailbreak detection logic at all, and if present, assess whether it's a simple, easily-bypassed check (a single file-existence test) versus a more layered, harder-to-defeat approach.
Assess whether any commercial or open-source obfuscator/RASP solution is applied at all, since even weak, defeatable protection is a materially different finding than none whatsoever.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes static/dynamic analysis of the test installation's binary.
Decompile the app and demonstrate the ease of obtaining readable logic for a security-sensitive routine (a certificate-pinning check, a biometric callback) as evidence.
Attach Frida and confirm unhindered ability to hook functions and modify runtime behavior at will.

Where feasible within the engagement's scope, chain this finding into a concrete demonstration of one of the app's other client-side findings to show the practical consequence of the missing protection.
Document the specific absence of protection observed across decompilation, debugging, and root/jailbreak-detection dimensions.

examplePayloads.label: Assess decompilation readability
examplePayloads.command: jadx -d decompiled_output target_app.apk  # check whether logic is fully readable without significant manual reconstruction

examplePayloads.label: Confirm unhindered Frida attachment
examplePayloads.command: frida -U -n com.target.app -l enumerate_classes.js  # attach and enumerate app classes without any anti-instrumentation trigger

examplePayloads.label: Check for the absence of any root/jailbreak detection
examplePayloads.command: frida -U -n com.target.app -l check_root_detection_calls.js  # search for and confirm absence of common root-check APIs

variants: Complete absence of any protection versus weak/outdated protection (a basic, single-check root-detection routine, or an old, publicly-defeated obfuscator) that provides negligible real-world resistance.

Obfuscation present but incomplete — string encryption and control-flow flattening applied to core logic while API keys or endpoint URLs remain in plaintext string constants, giving a reverse engineer an easy entry point despite the broader hardening effort.
mitigation: Apply a reputable commercial or well-maintained open-source obfuscation solution (ProGuard/R8 with aggressive settings at minimum, ideally a dedicated commercial obfuscator/RASP product for higher-sensitivity apps).
Implement layered root/jailbreak detection combining multiple independent indicators, understanding a sufficiently motivated attacker can still defeat any single-layer check.
Implement anti-debugging and anti-Frida countermeasures as defense in depth, accepting these raise attacker effort rather than providing an absolute guarantee.
Prioritize moving genuinely security-critical logic server-side rather than relying on binary protection alone to safeguard client-resident logic.

items.title: Pasteboard/Clipboard Leakage (iOS/Android)
items.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device. A clipboard-monitoring utility or script (adb-based, or a separate benign test app polling the OS clipboard API) to demonstrate cross-application visibility of copied content.
items.whatItIs: A 'copy to clipboard' feature copies sensitive data — a password, a one-time code, a full card number — to the system clipboard, and never clears it afterward, and doesn't use the platform's option to mark that content as sensitive (which some newer phones support). That leaves the value readable by any other app that can read the clipboard, and sometimes even saved in a clipboard history feature.
items.rootCause: The clipboard is a shared resource across the whole phone that basically any app can read from — this feature was built without accounting for that, and without using the specific flag some platforms offer to protect genuinely sensitive content from being read by other apps or saved in clipboard history.
items.impact: Any other app on the device can silently read the value while it sits on the clipboard, including malware or an over-permissioned app that monitors clipboard activity. Where the operating system keeps a clipboard history, the value can persist there and stay readable for longer than the app's own clearing timeout would suggest — assuming it has one at all.
stepsToIdentify: Trigger the app's copy-to-clipboard feature for a sensitive value.
From a separate, independent test app or via `adb shell service call clipboard`, poll the clipboard immediately after the copy operation and confirm the sensitive value is readable.
Measure how long the value remains on the clipboard before (if ever) the app clears it.

Check whether the app marks the clipped content as sensitive using the platform's dedicated flag (where the target API level supports it), which suppresses clipboard-history/preview surfacing even though the raw value technically remains readable to a polling app.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes clipboard-monitoring testing against the test installation.
Trigger the copy-to-clipboard action for a sensitive value within the app.
From a separate monitoring app/script, capture the clipboard content immediately and confirm the sensitive value is present.
Check whether the platform's clipboard-preview/history feature (if present on the test OS version) also surfaces the value.
Document the exact sensitive data type exposed, the duration it remained accessible, and whether the sensitive-content flag was applied.

examplePayloads.label: Monitor clipboard content from a separate process via adb
examplePayloads.command: adb shell service call clipboard 2 s16 com.android.shell

examplePayloads.label: Poll clipboard content from a benign test app after triggering the copy action in the target app
examplePayloads.command: # ClipboardManager.getPrimaryClip() polled from a separate test app immediately after switching from the target app

variants: Sensitive value persisted in OS-level clipboard history/preview (a longer-lived, separate exposure on platforms with this feature) versus only the immediate, single-slot clipboard buffer.
Value copied automatically without explicit user action as a side effect of another feature, increasing the chance of inadvertent exposure.
mitigation: Clear the clipboard automatically a short, fixed time after copying a sensitive value, and clear it immediately if the app is backgrounded before that timeout.
Use the platform's sensitive-clipboard-content API/flag where available to suppress clipboard preview/history surfacing of the copied value.
Minimize reliance on clipboard-based convenience features for highly sensitive values; where feasible, offer a masked, in-app "reveal" instead of a full clipboard copy.
Educate users, where the copy-to-clipboard feature is retained, that clipboard contents are shared system-wide and should be treated as temporarily exposed.
