OWASP MASTG-TEST-0028 (Testing for Sensitive Data in the Clipboard)

items.title: Root/Jailbreak Detection Bypass
items.prerequisites: A rooted/jailbroken test device or emulator with Frida and a root-hiding/bypass framework (Magisk Hide/Zygisk, or a Frida-based root-detection-bypass script set) available. The target application's decompiled code to locate its root/jailbreak-detection routine.
items.whatItIs: The app checks whether it's running on a rooted or jailbroken phone, and tries to restrict sensitive features if it is. But that check can be defeated using standard, publicly available tools — hooking the result of the check, using a well-known root-hiding tool, or just patching the check out of a modified copy of the app — letting the full, sensitive functionality run on a phone the developer specifically wanted to block.
items.rootCause: This kind of detection usually just looks for a small, well-known set of telltale signs — specific files, specific installed apps, specific system settings — and those are exactly what publicly available root-hiding tools are built to specifically hide or fake. Without extra layered protection around the check itself, it gets defeated by the same widely available tools that would beat almost any app relying on the same common checks.
items.impact: An attacker on a rooted or jailbroken device can defeat the app's attempt to restrict itself on exactly that kind of device. They then reach the sensitive functionality the developer deliberately withheld because of the elevated risk. The same root access also enables the attacks that restriction was meant to guard against, such as extracting protected secrets, hooking functions at runtime, and bypassing certificate pinning.
stepsToIdentify: Install and run the app on a rooted/jailbroken test device without any bypass tooling active, and confirm the app does detect the root/jailbreak state and restricts functionality as intended (establishing a baseline that detection exists at all).
Decompile the app to identify the specific indicators its detection logic checks for (file paths, package names, system properties).
Enable a standard root-hiding tool (Magisk Hide/Zygisk) or a Frida-based root-detection-bypass script and relaunch the app, observing whether the restriction is now bypassed.

Where the standard bypass doesn't immediately succeed, review whether the app's detection combines multiple independent indicators (making it more resistant) versus relying on a single, easily-spoofed check.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes root/jailbreak-detection bypass testing against the test installation on a rooted/jailbroken test device.
Confirm the baseline: the app detects and restricts functionality on the rooted device without any bypass active.
Enable a standard root-hiding tool or Frida bypass script and relaunch the app.
Confirm whether the previously-restricted sensitive functionality is now accessible.
Document the specific bypass technique that succeeded and the functionality it unlocked.

examplePayloads.label: Confirm baseline detection and restriction on an unmasked rooted device
examplePayloads.command: adb shell su -c 'echo test'  # confirm root access is present, then launch the app and observe its response

examplePayloads.label: Enable Magisk Hide/Zygisk for the target app package and retest
examplePayloads.command: # Magisk app: add com.target.app to the Zygisk/DenyList, then relaunch the app

examplePayloads.label: Standard Frida-based root-detection bypass
examplePayloads.command:
objection -g com.target.app explore
android root disable

variants: Detection relying on a single, easily-spoofed indicator versus a layered approach combining multiple checks that resists standard, generic bypass tooling but may still be defeated with more targeted, app-specific reverse engineering.
Detection present in the app itself but not paired with any server-side attestation (Play Integrity API/App Attest) that could independently flag the device state to the backend.
mitigation: Combine multiple independent root/jailbreak indicators rather than relying on any single, well-known check, increasing resistance to generic, off-the-shelf bypass tooling.

Use the platform's official integrity-attestation service (Google Play Integrity API, Apple's App Attest/DeviceCheck) to have the backend independently verify device integrity server-side, rather than relying solely on client-side detection that can itself be hooked/bypassed.
Apply anti-tampering protection specifically around the detection logic itself, so it can't simply be hooked or patched out via standard Frida scripting.

Accept that a sufficiently motivated attacker with a rooted/jailbroken device will likely eventually defeat any purely client-side detection, and ensure the most sensitive operations also have server-side verification independent of the client's self-reported device state.

items.title: Screen Caching / Sensitive UI Exposure
items.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device. Ability to trigger the OS's app-switcher/recent-apps view while the app displays representative sensitive data, and, for a rooted/jailbroken device, access to inspect any cached screenshot file the OS may have persisted.
items.whatItIs: When you switch away from the app (to another app or the home screen), the phone automatically takes a screenshot of whatever was on screen, to show in the recent-apps preview. If the app doesn't specifically hide its content right before this happens, sensitive information — an account balance, a message, a form full of personal data — ends up captured in that preview, and on some phones, even saved as a cached image file.
items.rootCause: This screenshot behavior is a standard phone feature the app doesn't control by default. Unless the app specifically opts in to hiding its content before going to the background (using a specific setting available on both major platforms), the screenshot just captures whatever was visible at that exact moment — including data the developer never intended to show up in a recent-apps preview or cached image.
items.impact: Anyone who can see the app-switcher view can read whatever was on screen when the app was backgrounded. That might be a bystander glancing over, or someone with brief access to an unlocked phone. Where the snapshot is also written to disk, an attacker with root access or a forensic tool can recover it long after the app has stopped running.
stepsToIdentify: Navigate to a screen displaying representative sensitive data within the app, then background the app (press home, or switch to another app) and open the OS app-switcher/recent-apps view.
Observe whether the sensitive data is visible in the app-switcher preview, versus the app showing a blank screen, its logo, or another obscured placeholder.
For a rooted/jailbroken test device, check the OS's cached-snapshot storage location for a persisted image file corresponding to the app and inspect its content directly.
Repeat across the app's various sensitive screens (not just the most obvious one), since obscuring behavior is sometimes applied inconsistently across different Activities/ViewControllers.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes app-switcher snapshot inspection on the test installation.
Navigate to a sensitive screen, populate it with representative test data, and background the app.
Open the app-switcher and document what sensitive content is visible in the preview.
On a rooted/jailbroken device, locate and inspect any persisted snapshot cache file for the same sensitive content.
Document each screen found to leak sensitive data via the app-switcher preview and/or a persisted cache file.

examplePayloads.label: Trigger backgrounding and app-switcher preview capture
examplePayloads.command: adb shell input keyevent KEYCODE_HOME && adb shell input keyevent KEYCODE_APP_SWITCH

examplePayloads.label: Locate a persisted app-switcher snapshot cache file (rooted device)
examplePayloads.command: adb shell find /data/system_ce/*/snapshots -iname '*com.target.app*'

variants: Sensitive content visible in the live app-switcher preview but not persisted to a long-lived cache file (lower severity) versus content that's both visible in the preview and recoverable from a persisted snapshot file well after the app session ends.
Obscuring correctly applied on the primary/most obvious sensitive screen (a login form) but missed on a secondary screen (an in-app messaging view) added later in development.
mitigation: Apply the platform's screen-obscuring mechanism (Android's `FLAG_SECURE` on the window, or an iOS technique of swapping in a blank/branded placeholder view during `applicationDidEnterBackground`) on every screen displaying sensitive data.
Audit all sensitive screens in the app for consistent application of this protection, since it's easy to apply it to the most obvious screen and miss a secondary one added later.

Where `FLAG_SECURE` is used on Android, be aware it also blocks screenshots/screen-recording generally, which is a related, complementary protection worth applying deliberately rather than as an afterthought.
Periodically re-verify this behavior after OS updates, since app-switcher snapshot behavior can change subtly between platform versions.

items.title: Sensitive Data in App Backups
items.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device with device-level backup enabled (Android's auto-backup or `adb backup`, iOS's iCloud/iTunes/Finder backup). Standard backup-extraction tooling (`adb backup`/`abe`, or an iOS backup-parsing tool like iMazing or a manual plist/SQLite extraction from an unencrypted iTunes backup) to inspect the resulting backup archive's content.
items.whatItIs: The app's data gets automatically included in the phone's normal backup system without the app specifically excluding sensitive files from it. That means a full phone backup — whether stored in the cloud or locally — contains the same sensitive data the app stores on the device (credentials, tokens, cached personal info), and it can be pulled out of that backup without ever needing the original phone at all.
items.rootCause: Phone backup systems include everything by default unless a developer specifically excludes certain files or folders. That exclusion step is easy to forget, especially for data the app started saving after the initial backup setup was already done.
items.impact: Anyone with access to a device backup can extract the app's data without ever touching the original phone or getting past its lock screen. That backup might come from a stolen device, a compromised cloud account, or something as ordinary as a shared family cloud login. The backup is an independent copy of the same data, so every protection built around the device itself is simply sidestepped.
stepsToIdentify: Review the app's backup configuration (Android's `android:allowBackup` manifest attribute and any associated backup-rules XML, or iOS's file-exclusion attributes on sensitive files) to determine what is and isn't excluded from backup.
Generate a representative device backup (`adb backup` for Android, or an unencrypted iTunes/Finder backup for iOS) after populating the app with representative sensitive test data.
Extract and inspect the backup archive's content for the app's data, confirming whether sensitive fields identified during local-storage testing are present in the backup.
Where the app does declare specific backup-exclusion rules, verify they cover every genuinely sensitive file/data location the app uses, not just the most obvious one.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes device-backup generation and extraction testing against the test installation.
Populate the app with representative sensitive test data.
Generate a device backup and extract the app's data from the resulting archive.
Inspect the extracted data for plaintext or trivially-recoverable sensitive content.
Document the exact backup mechanism used, the specific sensitive data recovered, and the current backup-exclusion configuration (if any).

examplePayloads.label: Generate an Android device backup and extract the app's data
examplePayloads.command:
adb backup -f app_backup.ab com.target.app
java -jar abe.jar unpack app_backup.ab app_backup.tar

examplePayloads.label: Inspect the extracted backup archive for sensitive content
examplePayloads.command: tar -xvf app_backup.tar && grep -r 'password\|token' apps/com.target.app/

examplePayloads.label: Check Android manifest for backup configuration
examplePayloads.command: apktool d target_app.apk -o decoded && grep -i 'allowBackup\|fullBackupContent' decoded/AndroidManifest.xml

variants: Sensitive data excluded from backup correctly for one storage location (SharedPreferences) but not another (a local SQLite database) within the same app.

Backup exclusion correctly configured, but a genuine platform-level secure-storage item (Keychain, in iOS's default configuration) is nonetheless included in an iCloud Keychain sync the user didn't realize extended that far, a related but distinct exposure path.
mitigation: Explicitly exclude all files/data containing sensitive information from the platform's backup mechanism (Android's backup-rules XML with a `<exclude>` directive, or the `NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey` file attribute on iOS).

Where backing up some app data is genuinely desirable for user convenience (restoring app state on a new device), ensure only non-sensitive data is included, with genuinely sensitive fields re-derived or re-authenticated after restore instead.
Audit backup-exclusion configuration whenever new sensitive storage locations are added to the app, since this is a common regression point.

Where the platform's backup encryption itself may be disabled by the user (an unencrypted local iTunes backup, for example), treat backup content as equivalent in sensitivity to unencrypted local device storage when assessing risk.

links: OWASP MASVS-STORAGE (MASVS-STORAGE-1: Sensitive Data on the Device)
OWASP MASTG-TEST-0005 (Testing Backups for Sensitive Data)

items.title: Sensitive Data in Logs
items.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device with access to its logs (via `adb logcat` for Android, or the Console app/log streaming for iOS on a development-provisioned or jailbroken device). No special privilege beyond standard debugging log access is required on most development/test configurations.
items.whatItIs: The app writes sensitive data — passwords, session tokens, API keys, personal user information — directly into the phone's system log during normal use. This is usually leftover debug logging from development that never got removed or properly disabled before the app was published.
items.rootCause: Detailed logging gets added generously during development to help with debugging, and logging a variable's full value — including sensitive ones — sticks around into the released version because nothing systematically checks for this before release. On top of that, on many phones, any app with basic log-reading permission (or sometimes no special permission at all) can read another app's log output.
items.impact: Any app able to read the system log can read the logged data directly, on the Android versions and configurations where that remains possible. So can anyone who receives a bug report or log export that a user or support process shares. This exposes credentials, tokens or personal data through a channel most users, and plenty of developers, never think to check when reviewing how the app handles sensitive data.
stepsToIdentify: Use the app normally (log in, perform typical sensitive actions) while capturing the device log via `adb logcat` (Android) or a log-streaming tool (iOS).
Search the captured log for the app's package/process tag and inspect for sensitive-looking content (credentials, tokens, PII fields) rather than assuming logs are automatically safe.
Confirm whether the identified logging occurs in every build variant (including release) or only in a debug-specific build flavor that shouldn't reach production.
Check whether a third-party SDK bundled in the app is the source of any sensitive logging, distinguishing first-party logging statements from a dependency's own verbose-logging default.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes device-log capture during normal use of the test installation.
Populate the app with representative sensitive test data through normal use while capturing the device log.
Search the captured log for the sensitive test data and confirm its presence in plaintext.

Where feasible, confirm cross-app log-read accessibility from a separate test app/adb session without special elevated privileges, to establish the practical exposure scope on the specific test device/OS version.
Document the exact log entries, the sensitive data type logged, and whether the issue is present in the release build specifically.

examplePayloads.label: Capture the device log while exercising the app's sensitive functionality
examplePayloads.command: adb logcat | grep -i 'com.target.app'

examplePayloads.label: Search a captured log for common sensitive-data patterns
examplePayloads.command: adb logcat -d | grep -iE 'password|token|api[_-]?key|ssn'

examplePayloads.label: Check whether logging occurs in the release build specifically
examplePayloads.command: grep -rn 'Log\.' decompiled_output/ | grep -v 'BuildConfig.DEBUG'

variants: Sensitive logging present only in a debug build flavor that was inadvertently distributed instead of the intended release build, versus logging present unconditionally regardless of build type.
Sensitive logging originating from a bundled third-party SDK's own verbose-logging default rather than first-party application code.
mitigation: Remove all logging of sensitive data from the codebase, or gate any genuinely necessary verbose logging behind a build-type check (`if (BuildConfig.DEBUG)`) that's guaranteed to be false in release builds.
Add automated static analysis to the CI/CD pipeline to flag logging statements referencing known-sensitive variable names/patterns before a release build is produced.
Review and configure third-party SDKs' logging verbosity explicitly, disabling verbose/debug logging in the production build configuration.
Where log data is genuinely needed for production diagnostics, redact/mask sensitive fields before logging rather than logging the raw value.

items.title: Tapjacking / Overlay Attacks (Android)
items.prerequisites: The target application and a second, malicious-simulation test app installed on the same Android test device. Ability to build a benign, clearly-labeled overlay test app using the `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW` permission to draw over the target app's UI.
items.whatItIs: A malicious app using Android's 'draw over other apps' permission can place an invisible or deceptive overlay on top of the real app's sensitive buttons — a login button, a permission prompt, a payment confirmation — tricking the user into thinking they're tapping the overlay's fake content, when their tap is actually registering on the real app's hidden button underneath. This works because the real app doesn't have any protection against being covered by an overlay.
items.rootCause: Android's 'draw over other apps' permission lets an app place persistent content on top of anything else, including sensitive screens. Unless the underlying app explicitly turns on a specific setting that ignores taps landing on an obscured view, a tap on a covered element is still delivered as a normal, valid tap — with no warning to the user that what they tapped may not have been what they saw.
items.impact: An attacker first gets the user to install a harmless-looking app that asks for the overlay permission — something users are well conditioned to grant for screen dimmers and floating widgets. That app can then cover the real app's buttons with deceptive content. The user taps what they think they see and unknowingly authorises something else: granting a dangerous permission, confirming a payment, or accepting a security prompt.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the app's most sensitive UI interactions — permission-grant dialogs, payment confirmations, security-setting toggles — as the priority targets for this check.
Decompile the app and check whether `setFilterTouchesWhenObscured(true)` (or the equivalent `android:filterTouchesWhenObscured` view attribute) is applied to these sensitive views.
Build or use an existing benign overlay test app (requesting `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW`) and, with the target app's sensitive screen in the foreground, draw a full-screen or targeted overlay over it.
Attempt to tap through the overlay at the location of the underlying sensitive button and confirm whether the tap registers on the target app despite the visual obstruction.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes overlay-based tapjacking testing against the test installation using a benign test overlay app.
Grant the test overlay app the `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW` permission (simulating a user who has granted this to a seemingly innocuous app).
Navigate the target app to a sensitive screen and activate the test overlay, positioned to visually obscure the sensitive button with deceptive content.

Tap at the screen location of the underlying sensitive button (as visually indicated by the overlay's deceptive prompt) and confirm whether the target app registers the tap as if the user had directly interacted with its real UI.
Document which specific sensitive UI elements lack overlay-touch-filtering protection and the resulting successful tapjacking demonstration.

examplePayloads.label: Check decompiled code for overlay-touch-filtering protection on sensitive views
examplePayloads.command: jadx -d decompiled_output target_app.apk && grep -rn 'setFilterTouchesWhenObscured\|filterTouchesWhenObscured' decompiled_output/

examplePayloads.label: Build a minimal overlay test app requesting SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW
examplePayloads.command: # minimal Android app: request SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, add a WindowManager overlay view with deceptive content positioned over the target app's known button coordinates

examplePayloads.label: Grant the overlay permission and activate the overlay for testing
examplePayloads.command: adb shell appops set com.test.overlayapp SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW allow

variants: Full-screen deceptive overlay versus a narrow, precisely-positioned overlay covering only the specific sensitive button, the latter being harder for a user to notice as suspicious.
Overlay attack targeting a system permission-grant dialog specifically (tricking the user into granting a dangerous permission to a different, malicious app) rather than an in-app sensitive action.
mitigation: Apply `setFilterTouchesWhenObscured(true)` (or the equivalent view attribute) to every sensitive interactive view in the app, causing Android to silently discard touch events delivered while the view is obscured by another app's overlay.
For the most sensitive confirmations, consider an additional, deliberate friction step (a swipe-to-confirm gesture, a re-authentication prompt) that's harder to trigger via a simple, redirected tap.

Educate users generally about the risk of granting the "draw over other apps" permission to unfamiliar apps, though this is a weaker, awareness-based mitigation relative to the app-side technical control.

Test overlay-touch-filtering protection on every new sensitive UI element added in future releases, since this is easy to miss for a newly-added button if it isn't part of an established, reviewed pattern.

items.title: Third-Party SDK / Library Vulnerabilities
items.prerequisites: The target application's APK/IPA for dependency extraction. A software-composition-analysis (SCA) tool (MobSF, OWASP Dependency-Check, or a mobile-specific SCA scanner) capable of identifying bundled third-party libraries/SDKs and their versions.
items.whatItIs: The app bundles third-party libraries or SDKs — analytics, ads, networking, UI components — at outdated versions that have known, publicly documented security bugs, because the app's dependency setup locks in a specific version once and there's no ongoing process to review and update it as new vulnerabilities get discovered.
items.rootCause: Third-party SDKs typically get integrated once and left alone unless a specific feature update is needed, since updating a dependency carries its own risk of something breaking and needing retesting. Without a dedicated, recurring process to review dependencies, the locked-in version quietly accumulates known, unpatched vulnerabilities over the app's lifetime — the same pattern that shows up with any outdated software dependency.
items.impact: Any known flaw in the outdated library becomes exploitable against the app, provided the app's own use of that library actually reaches the vulnerable code. The range is wide. It might sit in a code path the app never calls, which makes it low risk. Or it might be directly reachable, such as a TLS flaw in a networking library or a parsing bug in a data-handling one.
stepsToIdentify: Extract the list of bundled third-party libraries and their versions from the APK/IPA (via its dependency manifest, or by fingerprinting bundled library binaries/resources).
Run a software-composition-analysis tool against the extracted dependency list and review the resulting CVE findings, prioritizing Critical/High severity issues with a known public exploit.

For any Critical/High CVE found, assess reachability — whether the app's actual usage of the library invokes the vulnerable code path, or the vulnerable functionality is present but unused — to prioritize remediation accurately.
Cross-reference the library's pinned version against its current, actively-maintained release to quantify how far behind the integration has drifted.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes dependency extraction and SCA scanning of the test installation's app package.
Run the SCA tool against the extracted dependency list and record the full CVE findings list with severity ratings.
For the highest-severity, most-reachable finding, research whether a public proof-of-concept exists for that specific CVE in the context of a mobile app integration.

Where safe and clearly scoped, demonstrate the specific vulnerability against a non-production test build of the app (rather than the production release) to confirm real-world exploitability rather than relying on the scanner's severity rating alone.
Document the specific library, its version drift from current, and the prioritized CVE list with reachability assessment for the report.

examplePayloads.label: Run a mobile-focused software-composition-analysis scan against the APK
examplePayloads.command: mobsf-cli scan target_app.apk --format json > sca_results.json

examplePayloads.label: Fingerprint bundled library versions from extracted app resources
examplePayloads.command: unzip -o target_app.apk -d extracted && find extracted -iname '*.properties' -exec grep -H 'version' {} \;

examplePayloads.label: Cross-reference a specific bundled library's version against known CVEs
examplePayloads.command: grep -A5 '"library-name"' sca_results.json

variants: Vulnerable library present but its vulnerable code path not actually reachable by the app's specific usage pattern (lower practical risk despite a high CVSS score) versus one actively invoked in the app's core functionality.
Vulnerability introduced via a transitive dependency of a directly-integrated SDK, requiring dependency-tree-level scanning rather than only checking the top-level, directly-integrated libraries.
mitigation: Establish a recurring dependency-audit process (ideally automated via CI/CD-integrated SCA scanning) to catch newly-disclosed CVEs against bundled libraries promptly rather than only during periodic external assessments.
Update outdated third-party libraries/SDKs to their current, patched versions on a regular cadence, budgeting for the associated regression-testing effort as a routine maintenance cost.
Where a specific SDK has a poor security-maintenance track record, evaluate replacing it with a better-maintained alternative rather than continuing to accept its accumulating risk.
Maintain a software bill of materials (SBOM) for the app's bundled dependencies to make future vulnerability cross-referencing faster and more reliable.

links: OWASP MASTG-TEST-0039 (Testing for Weaknesses in Third-Party Libraries)

items.title: Insecure Backend-as-a-Service Security Rules
items.prerequisites: A mobile application using a backend-as-a-service platform for its database, storage or authentication. The application package, from which project identifiers and API keys can be extracted. A client or HTTP access to the platform's REST interface. Authorisation to query the backend directly using credentials recovered from the application.
items.whatItIs: These platforms let a mobile client talk to the database directly, which removes the server tier and with it the place authorisation usually lives. Access control instead lives in a rules document that the developer writes. Rules default to permissive during development, and the application works identically whether they were ever tightened, so the omission produces no symptom. The client's API key is embedded in the app and is not a secret.
items.rootCause: The development-friendly default is open access, and the documentation's quick-start reflects that. Tightening rules requires modelling every access pattern precisely, which is real work with no visible payoff, so it is deferred. Developers also frequently treat the embedded API key as a credential, when it identifies the project rather than authorising the caller. Rules changes are made in a console rather than in the repository, so they escape code review.
items.impact: Anyone who extracts the project identifier from the application — which requires only unzipping it — can query the backend directly, bypassing the app entirely. Where read rules are open the whole dataset is retrievable, and where write rules are open records can be modified or destroyed. Storage buckets with open rules disclose user-uploaded content. The access uses the platform's own API, so it appears as ordinary client traffic.
stepsToIdentify: Extract the application package and locate the platform configuration file containing project identifiers and keys.
Identify which platform services are in use: database, storage, authentication, functions.
Query the database REST endpoint unauthenticated and record whether data is returned.
Repeat as an authenticated but unprivileged user, since rules frequently distinguish only between signed-in and anonymous.
Enumerate storage paths and test whether objects are listable and readable without authorisation.
Test write access with a benign record, since read and write rules are configured independently.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers direct backend queries using identifiers recovered from the application.
Unzip the package and extract the platform configuration.
Issue an unauthenticated read against a collection path observed in the application's traffic or code.
Where reads succeed, establish the scope of exposure by counting records rather than retrieving them all.
Create an account through the application's normal registration and retry, since many rules only require any signed-in user.
Test a single benign write to a dedicated test path and remove it immediately, confirming write exposure without altering real data.

examplePayloads.label: Extract configuration
examplePayloads.command: unzip -o app.apk -d app_out && grep -rhoE '"project_id"|"firebase_url"|"storage_bucket"|apiKey' app_out/res app_out/assets 2>/dev/null | sort -u

examplePayloads.label: Unauthenticated database read
examplePayloads.command: curl -s 'https://<project>.firebaseio.com/.json?print=pretty' | head -40

examplePayloads.label: Collection read via REST
examplePayloads.command: curl -s 'https://firestore.googleapis.com/v1/projects/<project>/databases/(default)/documents/users'

examplePayloads.label: Storage listing
examplePayloads.command: curl -s 'https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/<bucket>/o'

examplePayloads.label: Authenticated-user retry
examplePayloads.command: # register through the app, then repeat the same reads with the resulting ID token

examplePayloads.label: Controlled write test
examplePayloads.command: curl -sX PUT 'https://<project>.firebaseio.com/pentest_marker.json' -d '{"probe":"MOB-RULES-1"}' && curl -sX DELETE 'https://<project>.firebaseio.com/pentest_marker.json'

variants: Rules requiring only an authenticated user, where anyone who registers reaches every user's data.
A storage bucket with open listing, disclosing uploaded documents and images belonging to all users.
Cloud functions callable directly without the authorisation the application performs client-side.
A second project used for staging with open rules and real data copied into it.
mitigation: Write rules that authorise per document against the requesting user's identity, and deny by default.
Treat the embedded API key as a public project identifier rather than as a credential.
Keep rules in version control and review them as code, rather than editing them in a console.
Test rules with the platform's emulator and rule-testing tooling as part of the build.
Apply the same rule discipline to storage paths, including listing permission.
Never copy production data into a project whose rules are relaxed for development.

items.title: Absent Device and App Attestation Allowing Modified Clients
items.prerequisites: A mobile application whose backend makes trust assumptions about the client, such as rate limits enforced in the app, client-side eligibility checks, or business flows assumed to require the real application. A rooted or jailbroken test device or emulator. Authorisation to run a modified client and to call backend endpoints directly.
items.whatItIs: Attestation is how a backend gains evidence that the request came from an unmodified application on a genuine device. Without it, the backend cannot distinguish its own app from a script replaying the same API calls. Root and jailbreak detection implemented inside the app does not fill the gap, because that check runs in the environment it is trying to assess and can be patched out. The distinction is whether the evidence is produced by something the attacker controls.
items.rootCause: Attestation requires backend integration and introduces failure modes on legitimate devices, so it is often skipped in favour of client-side checks that are cheap to add. Those checks feel equivalent because both produce a boolean, but one is self-reported. Where attestation is implemented, a common error is verifying the token in the app rather than at the server, which moves the decision back into the attacker's environment.
items.impact: Anything the backend delegates to the client stops being enforced: rate limits, eligibility rules, in-app purchase validation, promotional constraints. Automated abuse at scale becomes practical because the attacker needs no device at all once the API is understood. For applications with a financial or loyalty component, this is direct fraud exposure. It also invalidates the assumption that traffic reaching the API came from a user interacting with a screen.
stepsToIdentify: Determine whether the application requests any attestation token and whether the backend requires one.
Locate root or jailbreak detection in the binary and establish whether its result influences any server-side decision.
Identify which controls are enforced only in the client: rate limits, eligibility, validation of purchases.
Test whether backend endpoints accept requests from a plain HTTP client with no attestation token.
Where an attestation token is sent, determine whether the server validates it or merely logs it.
Check whether the token is bound to the specific request, or can be captured once and replayed.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers running a modified client and calling the API directly.
Intercept the application's traffic and record a normal request sequence for a controlled business flow.
Replay the sequence from a standalone client with no application present and record whether it succeeds.
Where a token is required, capture one and test whether it is accepted on a second, different request.
Patch out the client-side root detection and confirm the application functions, demonstrating the check is not server-enforced.
Demonstrate a client-side control being bypassed, choosing the least consequential available flow.

examplePayloads.label: Attestation usage check
examplePayloads.command: grep -rniE 'playintegrity|safetynet|attest|devicecheck|appattest' app_out/smali app_out/lib 2>/dev/null | head

examplePayloads.label: Direct API replay
examplePayloads.command: curl -sX POST https://api.example.test/v1/redeem -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"code":"PROMO"}'

examplePayloads.label: Token replay test
examplePayloads.command: # capture one attestation token and submit it with a different request body; record whether it is accepted

examplePayloads.label: Client-side rate limit bypass
examplePayloads.command: # issue requests faster than the app permits and record whether the server enforces any limit

examplePayloads.label: Root detection patch
examplePayloads.command: # use a hooking framework to force the detection routine to return false, then confirm the app proceeds

examplePayloads.label: Emulator acceptance
examplePayloads.command: # run the application on an emulator and record whether the backend behaves differently

variants: Attestation verified inside the application rather than at the server, which leaves the decision in the attacker's environment.
A token accepted without nonce binding, so one valid token authorises unlimited requests.
Attestation required on some endpoints and not others, where the unprotected ones do the same work.
Purchase receipts validated client-side, letting a modified client grant itself entitlements.
mitigation: Verify attestation tokens server-side, and require them on every endpoint where client integrity matters.
Bind each attestation token to a server-issued nonce and to the specific request, so tokens cannot be replayed.
Enforce rate limits, eligibility and validation server-side regardless of what the client does.
Validate purchase receipts against the store's server API rather than trusting the client.
Treat root and jailbreak detection as telemetry that raises suspicion, never as a control.
Decide deliberately how to handle attestation failure, since a permissive fallback removes the control entirely.

items.title: Insecure OAuth Redirect Handling in Mobile Applications
items.prerequisites: A mobile application authenticating through an OAuth or OpenID Connect flow that returns to the app via a custom URL scheme, app link or universal link. A test device where a second application can be installed to claim the same scheme. Authorisation to install a tester-built application and to intercept the authorisation response.
items.whatItIs: The authorisation code comes back to the application through a redirect, and on mobile the redirect target is a scheme or link the operating system routes. Custom schemes are not exclusive: any application can register the same one, and on Android the resolution when two apps claim a scheme is not guaranteed to favour the legitimate one. Without PKCE, an intercepted code can be exchanged for tokens by whoever holds it.
items.rootCause: Custom schemes were the original mobile redirect mechanism and remain common because they work everywhere without the domain verification that app links require. PKCE solves interception but is optional in many libraries and omitted in older integrations. Embedded web views are also still used despite giving the host application visibility of the credentials entered. The authorisation server frequently permits loose redirect matching, which widens the target.
items.impact: An attacker's application installed on the same device intercepts the authorisation code and exchanges it for the victim's tokens, yielding full account access without ever seeing a password. The victim's experience is a normal login, because the legitimate authorisation happened. Where an embedded web view is used, a malicious or compromised host application observes the credentials directly, which is worse than interception of a code.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the redirect mechanism: custom scheme, app link with domain verification, or an embedded web view.
Determine whether PKCE is used, and whether the code challenge method is SHA-256 rather than plain.
Check whether the state parameter is generated unpredictably and validated on return.
Where app links are used, verify that domain association is correctly published and validated.
Test whether a second application registering the same scheme can receive the redirect.
Review the authorisation server's registered redirect URIs for wildcards or loose matching.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers installing a tester application on the test device.
Capture a complete authorisation flow and record the redirect URI, state and any code challenge.
Build a minimal application registering the same custom scheme and install it alongside the target.
Initiate authentication in the target application and record which application receives the redirect.
Where the code is intercepted, attempt the token exchange, which succeeds without PKCE and fails with it.
Report the redirect mechanism, PKCE status and interception result together, since the severity depends on the combination.

examplePayloads.label: Find registered schemes
examplePayloads.command: grep -A3 -E 'android.intent.action.VIEW' app_out/AndroidManifest.xml | grep -oE 'android:scheme="[^"]+"' | sort -u

examplePayloads.label: Check PKCE usage
examplePayloads.command: # inspect the authorization request for code_challenge and code_challenge_method=S256

examplePayloads.label: Competing scheme registration
examplePayloads.command: <intent-filter><action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW"/><data android:scheme="myapp"/></intent-filter>

examplePayloads.label: Capture the redirect
examplePayloads.command: adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d 'myapp://callback?code=TEST&state=TEST'

examplePayloads.label: Token exchange attempt
examplePayloads.command: curl -sX POST https://idp.example.test/oauth/token -d 'grant_type=authorization_code&code=<intercepted>&client_id=<id>&redirect_uri=myapp://callback'

examplePayloads.label: App link verification
examplePayloads.command: adb shell pm get-app-links <package>

variants: An embedded web view rather than the system browser, letting the host application observe credentials directly.
A loosely matched redirect URI at the authorisation server, permitting a redirect to an attacker-controlled path.
A public client with an embedded client secret, which is recoverable from the package.
State omitted or predictable, permitting cross-site request forgery against the authorisation flow.
mitigation: Use PKCE with the SHA-256 challenge method on every mobile authorisation request.
Prefer verified app links or universal links over custom schemes, since domain verification makes the target exclusive.
Use the system browser or a secure custom tab rather than an embedded web view.
Generate state unpredictably and validate it on return, rejecting mismatches.
Register exact redirect URIs at the authorisation server and disable wildcard matching.
Treat the mobile client as public: never embed a client secret and never rely on one for security.

items.title: Content Provider Injection and Path Traversal (Android)
items.prerequisites: An Android application exposing a content provider, whether explicitly exported or reachable through a granted URI permission. A test device and a tester-built application to act as the querying client. Authorisation to query the provider from another application and to attempt parameter injection against it.
items.whatItIs: A content provider is an interface other applications can query, and the query parameters — selection strings, sort order, projection — are frequently passed into a database query with string concatenation. That is SQL injection with an inter-application interface as the entry point. File-backed providers have the analogous problem: a path supplied by the caller is resolved without normalisation, so traversal reaches files outside the intended directory.
items.rootCause: The provider API hands the developer a selection string and a sort order, which invites concatenation into the query. Selection arguments exist to parameterise this but are optional and frequently unused. Providers are sometimes exported unintentionally, since older Android versions defaulted to exported when an intent filter was present. File providers resolve caller-supplied paths against a base directory without canonicalising first, which traversal defeats.
items.impact: A malicious application installed on the device reads the target application's private database, which commonly holds session tokens, personal data and cached records. Injection into the selection clause reaches tables the provider never intended to expose. Path traversal in a file provider reads arbitrary files in the application's sandbox, including shared preferences and credential caches. All of this requires no special permission on the attacking application.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate providers declared in the manifest and record which are exported and what permissions they require.
Identify providers exported implicitly, including those reachable through granted URI permissions.
Determine the authority and the URI paths the provider serves.
Query the provider from a separate application and record whether access is permitted.
Test whether the selection, projection and sort parameters are concatenated by supplying values with SQL metacharacters.
For file-backed providers, test whether traversal sequences in the path escape the intended directory.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers querying the provider from a tester-built application on the test device.
Enumerate provider authorities and attempt a baseline query to establish reachability.
Inject a condition into the selection parameter and observe whether the result set changes, which proves concatenation.
Use the projection parameter to reach columns or tables outside the provider's intended exposure.
For a file provider, request a path with traversal sequences and confirm whether a file outside the base directory is returned.
Record what was retrievable by category rather than extracting personal data in bulk.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate providers
examplePayloads.command: grep -E '<provider' -A6 app_out/AndroidManifest.xml

examplePayloads.label: Baseline query
examplePayloads.command: adb shell content query --uri content://com.example.app.provider/records

examplePayloads.label: Selection injection
examplePayloads.command: adb shell content query --uri content://com.example.app.provider/records --where "1=1) OR (1=1"

examplePayloads.label: Projection abuse
examplePayloads.command: adb shell content query --uri content://com.example.app.provider/records --projection "* FROM sqlite_master--"

examplePayloads.label: File provider traversal
examplePayloads.command: adb shell content read --uri content://com.example.app.fileprovider/files/../shared_prefs/session.xml

examplePayloads.label: Automated provider testing
examplePayloads.command: drozer console connect -c "run app.provider.query content://com.example.app.provider/records"

variants: A provider protected by a permission declared at normal rather than signature level, which any application can request.
A grant-URI-permission path that is broader than intended, exposing more than the shared item.
An openFile implementation that resolves a caller-supplied path without canonicalisation.
A provider that is not exported but is reachable through an exported activity acting as a proxy.
mitigation: Set exported to false explicitly on every provider that does not need to serve other applications.
Protect necessary providers with a signature-level permission so only the developer's own applications can query them.
Use parameterised selection arguments and never concatenate caller-supplied values into a query.
Validate the projection against an allowlist of permitted columns rather than passing it through.
Canonicalise any caller-supplied path and confirm it resolves inside the intended directory before opening it.
Expose the narrowest surface the use case requires, rather than a general-purpose query interface over the database.

items.title: Sensitive Data Retained in Application Memory
items.prerequisites: A mobile application handling credentials, tokens, payment details or personal data. A rooted or jailbroken test device permitting process memory access, or the ability to capture a memory dump. Authorisation to dump and search process memory, and a handling procedure for any sensitive values recovered.
items.whatItIs: Values are protected carefully on disk and in transit and then left in memory indefinitely. Strings in managed runtimes are immutable, so a password held in a string cannot be overwritten and persists until garbage collection happens to reclaim it, which may be long after the login screen closed. Anything in memory is recoverable from a process dump, and on a compromised device that is a straightforward operation.
items.rootCause: Language runtimes do not provide a way to erase an immutable string, and the byte-array alternatives are awkward enough that developers use strings anyway. Values are also copied during normal processing — into logs, into UI state, into serialisation buffers — so even careful clearing of the original leaves copies behind. Memory hygiene has no visible effect in testing, so it is rarely prioritised.
items.impact: On a rooted or compromised device, or via a crash dump collected by a diagnostics service, credentials and tokens are recoverable long after the user believed the session ended. This defeats the protection given to the same values at rest, since the memory copy is unencrypted by definition. Where payment data is involved the retention itself may breach the applicable standard, independent of whether anyone extracted it.
stepsToIdentify: Identify which sensitive values the application handles and at what point each should no longer be needed.
Establish whether values are held as immutable strings or as clearable byte arrays.
Dump process memory after authentication and search for marker credentials used during the test.
Repeat after logout and after backgrounding the application, to determine whether values are cleared on those transitions.
Check whether crash reporting captures memory regions, since that transmits the same data off the device.
Determine whether the application requests exclusion from memory capture where the platform supports it.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers memory dumping and agree how recovered values will be handled and destroyed.
Authenticate with distinctive marker credentials so recovered values are unambiguous and not real.
Dump the process memory while the session is active and search for the markers.
Log out within the application, dump again, and record whether the markers persist.
Background the application, wait, dump again, and record persistence across the lifecycle.
Report which value types persist and for how long, rather than reproducing recovered values.

examplePayloads.command: strings -n 8 /tmp/app.dump | grep -c 'MARKER-MOB-5'

variants: Tokens retained after logout because only the on-disk copy is cleared.
Payment card data persisting in memory after the transaction completes.
Sensitive values captured in a heap dump uploaded by a crash reporting service.
Decrypted database contents held in memory long after the records were displayed.
mitigation: Hold secrets in mutable byte arrays and overwrite them explicitly once they are no longer needed.
Minimise the lifetime of sensitive values, clearing them at the earliest point rather than at session end.
Clear credentials and tokens on logout and when the application is backgrounded, not only on process termination.
Use platform key stores for cryptographic operations so key material never enters application memory.
Exclude sensitive regions from crash reports, or disable memory capture in crash reporting entirely.
Accept that memory protection is mitigation rather than prevention on a compromised device, and pair it with server-side session controls.

items.title: Sensitive Input Cached by Keyboards, Autofill and Predictive Text
items.prerequisites: A mobile application with input fields receiving sensitive data: credentials, payment details, identifiers or personal information. A test device where the keyboard's learned dictionary and autofill store can be inspected, which may require root or a backup extraction. Authorisation to inspect keyboard caches and autofill stores.
items.whatItIs: Text typed into an application does not stay within it. The keyboard is a separate application that receives every keystroke, and unless the field is marked appropriately it adds words to a learned dictionary to improve prediction. Autofill frameworks may store field contents. Third-party keyboards can transmit what they learn to their own servers. So a value the application protects carefully can end up cached by software the developer never chose.
items.rootCause: Learning is the keyboard's default behaviour because prediction is its purpose, and the application must opt out per field using the correct input type or flag. Developers set input types for keyboard layout rather than for privacy, so a field configured for a numeric pad may still be learned. Autofill participation is likewise opt-out per field. Users install third-party keyboards freely, and the application has no control over what they do.
items.impact: Sensitive values persist in a store the application cannot reach and does not clear, surviving application uninstall and appearing as suggestions in unrelated applications — which is also how the exposure is typically discovered. On a shared or compromised device the cache is readable directly. Where a third-party keyboard transmits learned text, the data leaves the device to a party the organisation never assessed, which is a disclosure independent of any attacker.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate input fields receiving sensitive data and record the input type and flags set on each.
Confirm whether password and sensitive fields use an input type that disables suggestions and learning.
Check whether autofill is disabled on fields where it should not participate.
Type distinctive marker values into each field and then check whether they appear as suggestions elsewhere.
Inspect the keyboard's learned dictionary directly where device access permits.
Determine whether the application warns about or restricts third-party keyboards on sensitive screens.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers inspecting keyboard and autofill stores on the test device.
Enter unique marker values into each sensitive field through normal application use.
Open an unrelated application and begin typing the marker prefix to see whether it is suggested.
Where device access permits, inspect the keyboard dictionary and autofill store directly for the markers.
Record which fields leaked and which did not, since the difference identifies the misconfigured ones.
Report per field, because remediation is a per-field attribute change rather than a global setting.

examplePayloads.label: Review input types
examplePayloads.command: grep -E 'inputType|importantForAutofill|textNoSuggestions' -r app_out/res/layout | grep -i -E 'password|card|pin|ssn'

examplePayloads.label: Correct password configuration
examplePayloads.command: android:inputType="textPassword"   android:importantForAutofill="no"

examplePayloads.label: Numeric sensitive field
examplePayloads.command: android:inputType="numberPassword"   <!-- not "number", which is still learned -->

examplePayloads.label: Marker entry

examplePayloads.label: Suggestion check
examplePayloads.command: # in an unrelated app, type MARKER and record which markers are offered as suggestions

examplePayloads.label: Dictionary inspection
examplePayloads.command: adb shell run-as <keyboard.package> ls -la databases/ 2>/dev/null   # requires a debuggable keyboard or root

variants: A third-party keyboard transmitting learned text to its own servers, taking the data off the device entirely.
Autofill storing payment or identity values in a store shared across applications.
Clipboard retention where the user copies a sensitive value and it remains available to other applications.
An iOS field lacking the secure text entry flag, leaving it subject to the same learning behaviour.
mitigation: Set an input type that disables suggestions and learning on every sensitive field, including numeric ones.
Disable autofill participation on fields that should not be stored, using the platform's per-field attribute.
Use secure text entry on iOS for sensitive fields, which also suppresses learning.
Clear the clipboard after a sensitive value is copied, and avoid offering copy on such fields.
Consider restricting third-party keyboards on high-sensitivity screens where the platform allows it.
Test with markers as part of release testing, since the misconfiguration is per field and easy to reintroduce.
